- **Ground lenses** [`lenses`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/lenses.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. Spectacle makers grind ordinary lenses. Clear, streak-free glass and long-focus objectives are the bottleneck; the best come from Rome and Augsburg. Local: Vienna spectacle makers; Bohemian and Venetian glass on the market. Elsewhere: Rome: Giuseppe Campani, Eustachio Divini; Augsburg: optical workshops in the tradition of Johann Wiesel; The Hague: Christiaan and Constantijn Huygens.

- **Law of refraction, image formation and vision** [`refraction_optics`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/refraction_optics.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Kepler's Dioptrice and the sine law are in the Jesuit mathematicians' books. Lens makers work by trial; nobody computes a lens before grinding it. - **Camera obscura** [`camera_obscura`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/camera_obscura.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Known from Scheiner and Kircher as a way to watch sunspots and eclipses and as a painter's aid. Portable box versions are described in books. Local: Kircher, Ars magna lucis et umbrae (1646, 2nd ed. 1671).
- **Microscope** [`microscope`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/microscope.md) — K2, use partial, make medium, accept medium. Compound 'flea glasses' are cabinet curiosities. Kircher claimed to see 'worms' in plague blood (1658). Leeuwenhoek's tiny single lens and its method are unknown here. Local: Kircher, Scrutinium pestis (1658), read after the plague of 1679; physicians of the medical faculty. Elsewhere: Delft: Leeuwenhoek, single-lens microscopes, method kept secret; London: Hooke, Micrographia (1665); Rome: Campani and Divini; Augsburg: instrument makers.
- **Telescope (refractor)** [`telescope`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/telescope.md) — K3, use correct, make medium, accept high. Officers carry draw-tube spyglasses; a lookout watches from St Stephen's tower. Astronomical use is rare: Vienna has no observatory and no maker of long objectives. Local: lookout in the tower of St Stephen's; Jesuit college and university. Elsewhere: Rome: Campani's long telescopes; Paris Observatory: Cassini; Danzig: Hevelius; Augsburg: telescope makers; The Hague: Huygens's aerial telescope (published 1684).
- **Reflecting telescope** [`reflecting_telescope`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/reflecting_telescope.md) — K1, use none, make hard, accept medium. Newton's small reflector (1668, reported 1672) is hearsay. Bell founders can cast speculum metal; figuring and polishing the mirror, which also tarnishes, is the difficulty. Local: bell and gun founders (tin-rich bronze). Elsewhere: Cambridge and London: Newton, Royal Society.
- **Achromatic lens** [`achromatic_lens`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/achromatic_lens.md) — K0, use none, make very-hard, accept medium. Coloured fringes are fought with very long focal lengths. No dense lead glass of optical quality exists here; Ravenscroft's lead crystal is new in London. Elsewhere: London: George Ravenscroft's lead glass (1670s), not yet used for optics.
- **Spectrum and the nature of colour** [`spectrum_colour`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/spectrum_colour.md) — K1, use none, make easy, accept medium. Colours are held to be white light weakened or mixed with darkness (Aristotle, Kircher). Newton's 1672 paper is disputed even in London. Glass prisms are sold as toys. Local: Marcus Marci's prism experiments, Thaumantias (Prague 1648). Elsewhere: Cambridge: Newton.
- **Spectral analysis** [`spectroscopy`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/spectroscopy.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept low
- **Waves - sound and light** [`wave_nature_light_sound`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/wave_nature_light_sound.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Sound as motion of air is accepted (bell in a vacuum, in Schott). Light is a quality or Cartesian pressure; Grimaldi's diffraction (1665) is known, Huygens's waves are unpublished. Local: Kircher, Musurgia (1650) and Phonurgia nova (1673). Elsewhere: The Hague: Huygens, wave theory presented in Paris 1678, printed 1690.
- **Finite speed of light** [`speed_of_light`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/speed_of_light.md) — K1, use none, make hard, accept low. Rømer's delay of Jupiter's moon (Paris 1676) is contested by Cassini himself. Cartesians and scholastics hold light to be instantaneous. Elsewhere: Paris Observatory: Rømer until 1681, then Copenhagen.
- **Photography** [`photography`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/photography.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept medium. Apothecaries sell silver dissolved in aqua fortis (lunar caustic) and know it blackens skin; the cause is put down to air or heat. No fixing agent is known. Local: apothecaries; mint assayers (aqua fortis, silver).

Archimedes, Stevin and Pascal are in the textbooks; assayers and brewers use the balance and floats. A press built on Pascal's principle does not exist. Local: mint assayers; Schott, Mechanica hydraulico-pneumatica (1657).
- **Falling bodies and projectiles** [`falling_bodies`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/falling_bodies.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Galileo's law of fall was confirmed by the Jesuit Riccioli (1651) and is taught. Gunners still lay pieces by quadrant and experience tables; air resistance is ignored. Local: imperial gunners (Büchsenmeister) of the arsenal. Elsewhere: Paris: Blondel, L'art de jetter les bombes (1683).
- **Laws of motion** [`laws_of_motion`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/laws_of_motion.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept medium. The university teaches Aristotelian motion with impetus. Descartes's inertia is known but his works are on the Index (1663). Force equals mass times acceleration is stated nowhere. Elsewhere: Cambridge: Newton (unpublished until 1687); The Hague: Huygens, laws of collision and centrifugal force.
- **Universal gravitation** [`universal_gravitation`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/universal_gravitation.md) — K0, use none, make hard, accept low. Weight is a tendency towards the Earth's centre; planets move by vortices or angels. Hooke has guessed an inverse-square pull; Newton has the proof in a drawer. Elsewhere: London: Hooke, Halley, Wren discuss the inverse square (1684); Cambridge: Newton.
- **Strength of materials and scaling** [`strength_of_materials`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/strength_of_materials.md) — K2, use partial, make easy, accept high. Master builders and fortress engineers size beams, vaults and gun carriages by rules of proportion. Galileo's beam theory (1638) is read by few; nobody tests samples. Local: fortress engineers; master masons and carpenters. Elsewhere: London: Hooke's law of the spring (1678); Paris: Mariotte's bending and pipe-bursting tests.

- **Pendulum clock** [`pendulum_clock`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/pendulum_clock.md) — K3, use correct, make medium, accept high. Pendulum clocks have reached German and Austrian workshops since the 1660s, mostly with verge escapement and short pendulum. Anchor escapement and seconds pendulum are English novelties. Local: Vienna clockmakers. Elsewhere: The Hague: Huygens; London: anchor escapement, long-case clocks; Augsburg; Sobieski's court: the Jesuit clockmaker Adam Kochański.
- **Air pressure and the barometer** [`atmospheric_pressure`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/atmospheric_pressure.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Torricelli's tube and Guericke's shows are known from Schott's books. Many Jesuit philosophers still deny a true void and speak of subtle matter. Mercury is plentiful. Local: mercury from the imperial mine at Idrija; glassmakers for tubes; Schott, Mechanica hydraulico-pneumatica (1657), Technica curiosa (1664). Elsewhere: Hamburg: Otto von Guericke (aged 80); London: Boyle; Florence: Viviani, Torricelli's pupil.
- **Air pump and vacuum experiments** [`air_pump_vacuum`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/air_pump_vacuum.md) — K2, use none, make medium, accept medium. Guericke showed his pump to the Imperial Diet at Regensburg in 1654; it went to the Würzburg Jesuits. Brass founders can cast a barrel; seals and valves are the craft. - **Thermometer and temperature scale** [`thermometer_temperature`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/thermometer_temperature.md) — K3, use partial, make medium, accept medium. - **Specific and latent heat** [`latent_specific_heat`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/latent_specific_heat.md) — K0, use none, make medium, accept medium. Heat and temperature are not told apart; without comparable thermometers nobody can measure either.

- **Weather instruments and forecasting** [`weather_instruments`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/weather_instruments.md) — K2, use partial, make medium, accept medium. Printed calendars forecast weather from the stars. Guericke's water barometer with a floating manikin and his storm warning of 1660 are in his book; nobody here keeps daily readings. - **Heliocentric model** [`heliocentrism`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/heliocentrism.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept low. Copernicus is on the Index since 1616; it may be used as a calculating hypothesis only. The Jesuits teach Tycho's system after Riccioli. Arguing it as truth risks a denunciation. Local: Jesuit faculty of philosophy; Riccioli, Almagestum novum (1651). Elsewhere: Protestant universities, Holland, England: taught openly.
- **Kepler's laws of planetary motion** [`keplers_laws`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/keplers_laws.md) — K3, use partial, make medium, accept medium. Kepler served three emperors and his tables are in use, so the ellipse is accepted as a computing device. The area law is often replaced by easier approximations. Local: Rudolphine Tables; Kepler's years in Prague and Linz as imperial mathematician.
- **Distances of Moon, Sun and stars (parallax)** [`astronomical_distances`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/astronomical_distances.md) — K2, use partial, make hard, accept medium. The Moon's distance is known; for the Sun old values twenty times too small still circulate. Cassini and Richer's Mars parallax (1672) is recent Paris news. Elsewhere: Paris Observatory: Cassini.
- **Comets as orbiting bodies** [`comets_orbits`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/comets_orbits.md) — K2, use partial, make medium, accept medium. The great comet of 1680 and that of 1682 were preached as heralds of the Turk. Scholars accept comets are beyond the Moon; a returning orbit is nobody's idea yet. Local: comet pamphlets and sermons of 1680–1682. Elsewhere: Plauen: Dörffel's parabola for the comet of 1680 (1681); London: Halley observed the comet of 1682; Danzig: Hevelius, Cometographia (1668).
